In this experiment your task is to judge which of the red bricks would fall off the table if the black brick wasn't there (see the example images below).

First image: an example of a pile of bricks you may see in the experiment. Second image: the selected white bricks are the ones that the person thought would fall off the table if the black brick wasn't there.

In the original study, participants first gained experience with the physical properties of the bricks by seeing bricks fall on the table. You will then see 43 different piles of bricks. For each pile, please select the red bricks that you think would fall off the table if the black brick hadn't been there. Note that each pile is stable. That is, none of the red bricks would fall off the table if the black brick remained where it is.

The original study also included catch trials throughout the experiment and an attention check at the end.

In this experiment your task is to judge how many of the red bricks would fall off the table if the black brick wasn't there (see the example image below).

You will then make judgments for 43 different piles of bricks. Note that each pile is stable. That is, none of the red bricks would fall off the table if the black brick remained where it is.

In this experiment your task is to judge to what extent the black brick is responsible for the red bricks staying on the table (see the example image below).

You will then make responsibility judgments for 43 different piles of bricks. Note that each pile is stable. That is, none of the red will fall off the table if nothing happens.
